sentences.text: It became, that summer, a slightly unreasonable interest.
Her mother's word for it was *fixation*, said fondly in June and less fondly by the third week of July.
Ada is prepared to admit this now.
She kept a notebook.
She wrote down times: first bird of the evening, last bird, direction of the loops.
She got a library book that was too old for her and read the parts she could.
She annoyed her mother by explaining swift digestion at dinner on four separate occasions.
The question that would not leave her alone was the sleeping.
She could accept the flying.
Flying is what wings are for.

But the idea that a creature could be asleep — properly asleep, off, gone — two kilometres up in the dark, and continue to fly, seemed to her to be a much bigger claim than anybody was treating it as.
She asked Mr Iqbal how it worked.
He was in the yard when she asked, in the deckchair he kept behind the bin store, with the telescope pointed at the same nothing as always.
"Nobody entirely knows," he said, with enormous satisfaction.
"The current thinking is that half the brain sleeps and the other half keeps an eye on things, and then they swap.
Dolphins do something similar.
But if you are asking me whether anyone has been up there at two in the morning and watched — no.
They have not.

There are radar traces and there is a French pilot in 1914 who flew into a lot of them at two thousand metres at night and never got over it, and that is roughly the state of human knowledge." "So it might be something else." "It might be anything at all," said Mr Iqbal.
"That is the good news." Ada started going out on the fire escape at eleven, which was permitted, and at two, which was not.
She thought about the French pilot for weeks.
She looked him up in the end, at the library, on a computer with a sticky keyboard.
There was not much.
A few lines, repeated in several places, all of them obviously copied from each other.
A reconnaissance flight at night in 1914.
Two thousand metres over the lines.
He had cut the engine to glide, and come down through an enormous number of birds, and in the silence he could hear them all round him, and they were not visible and were not disturbed by him.
What got her was the detail about cutting the engine.
He had not been looking for anything.

He had switched off for some ordinary practical reason, in a war, at night, and in the quiet that followed he had found out something true about the world that nobody on the ground knew — and then had had to land, and had had nobody to tell, and had written it down anyway.
She wrote *1914* on the inside cover of the notebook and did not explain it to anybody.
She never saw one at two.
Of course she didn't; they were two thousand metres up.
But she went out anyway and stood in the cold with her head back, and there was the orange sky over the retail park, and the aerial, and the one tree, and nothing.
And she knew that they were up there.
Directly up there.
Above the flats, above the retail park, above the whole ridiculous orange glow of it, going round in slow circles in the actual dark with half of themselves asleep.

She has said since that this was the first time in her life she understood that something can be completely true and completely invisible at the same time, and that the two facts have nothing to do with each other.
She tested the idea on other things for about a month, which is what you do when you are eleven and have got hold of a good one.
The water in the pipes in the wall of her bedroom, going somewhere, all night.
The tectonic plate under the retail park, moving at the speed a fingernail grows.
Whatever was in the sealed flat on the third floor that nobody had opened since Mrs Kaur died.
The fact that on the other side of the world it was Wednesday afternoon and a very large number of people were having an ordinary day she would never hear a single detail of.
Some of these worked better than others.
Mr Iqbal was given all of them and rated them.
